title: Lamp of beauty
hookLine: the Jaap moves into Persian: He is the glorious one, the lamp of beauty (Jaap)

lines: SOME THINGS SOUND RIGHT IN ONE.
cards: A friend who speaks three languages is telling you a story in English. Then they reach the part they really care about, and suddenly it's Spanish, or Punjabi, or Tagalog.
Some things only sound right in one language: grandma's words, the word for that kind of evening. Partway through Jaap Sahib, the Tenth Guru does something like that.
He moves into Persian, the language of poets and courts, and starts talking about beauty.

teach.h: PERSIAN: THE LANGUAGE OF COURTS AND POETS.
teach.b: In the Tenth Guru's world, Persian was the language of the Mughal court, of government papers, and of a great tradition of love poetry. The Guru knew it well; his letter to the emperor, the Zafarnama, is written in it.

So when Jaap moves into Persian and Arabic words, it isn't showing off. It reaches for a language with a long habit of praising beauty. The lines begin with a little word, ki, meaning something like: for You are.
One of them says the One is husnal charaag.
Husn is beauty, the same word Punjabi still uses for a lovely face or a lovely view. Charaag, or chiragh, is a small oil lamp of the kind that lit houses and shrines. The lamp of beauty.

teach.h: A LAMP LETS YOU SEE EVERYTHING ELSE.
teach.b: A lamp isn't beautiful because of its own shape; it's beautiful because it lets you see everything else. Lamplight makes a room golden.
So the line suggests that beauty itself has a source, and that every lovely thing is lit by it.
In the same Persian stretch, Jaap uses names like kareem, generous, and raheem, merciful, names Muslims also use for God.
The Tenth Guru brings them into Sikh morning prayer without hesitating.
Jaap reaches for every language the Guru had, Braj, Sanskrit, Persian, Arabic, as if to say: no single tongue holds the One, and every tongue can praise.

how: Sikhs reciting Jaap Sahib move through its Persian and Arabic passages each morning in the same rhythm as the rest, and the words husn (beauty) and charaag (lamp) are still familiar in Punjabi.

o: a Persian love poem praising a beloved face
a golden lamp kept burning in a gurdwara
the lamp of beauty, lighting every lovely thing

games.q: lamp of beauty — tap the pairs.

s: Jaap Sahib is written entirely in Punjabi
it mixes Braj, Sanskrit-style words, Persian and Arabic; today's lines are Persian.
the Tenth Guru's letter to the emperor was written in Persian
the Zafarnama: Persian was the language of the Mughal court.
Jaap uses names like kareem and raheem
generous and merciful, names Muslims also use for God.

games.q: you want to praise beauty, and you know several languages. which does the Tenth Guru reach for in this stretch of Jaap?
o: Persian, the language of courts and love poetry.
games.why: Jaap switches into Persian and Arabic words here, and calls the One husnal charaag, the lamp of beauty.

practice: Find one beautiful thing near you, the grain in a table, light on a wall, the curve of a mug handle, someone's handwriting, and rest your eyes on it.
Then notice the light that's letting you see it, a window, a lamp, a screen's glow, and breathe slowly with the two together. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, the word of wonder.

wordCard.voice: Husnal charaag. Husn is beauty; charaag, a lamp — the One as the lamp that lets every lovely thing be seen.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: husn, beauty, a Persian word still used in Punjabi; Jaap's husnal charaag is the lamp of beauty.

carryVoice: Your line: makes a room golden. The lamp is what lets the beauty show. Day three hundred forty-four.
